The Salt Road

In which Ines finally crosses the flats.

The tide had gone out in the night and taken the sound with it. Ines stood at the edge of the causeway with her boots in her hand, listening to a silence so complete she could hear the salt drying on her sleeves.

“You’ll want to start now,” said the ferryman, who had not looked up from his knots. “The flats are kind for about four hours. After that they remember what they are.”

She had been told the road was marked. It was, in a way: every hundred paces, a post of black oak leaned out of the mud like a tired man, each one carved with a single letter. S, then A, then L. By the third post she understood that the road was spelling something, and by the fifth she decided she did not want to know what.

Her mother had crossed it once, in the year before the water changed. She never spoke of it, except to say that you should walk the way you read—slowly, and without moving your lips.

* * *

Halfway out, the mud began to hold her. Not roughly. It was more the way a hand holds a hand, and Ines found she could not tell whether it was asking her to stay or only wished to be remembered. She sat on a post, put her boots back on, and wrote the first line of the letter she had been avoiding for three weeks
